title: Sanskrit as a language of learning and courts across Asia
summary: Sanskrit, an Indo-European language whose oldest form is Vedic Sanskrit, reached its classical form around 500 BCE. Around the beginning of the Common Era this long-sacred language was remade as a medium of literature and political expression, and Sanskrit literary culture spread from Afghanistan to Java. For almost a thousand years, roughly 300 to 1300 CE, it was the prestige language of the South Asian subcontinent and much of Southeast Asia, until local languages displaced it in literature and politics from about the start of the second millennium.

uncertainty.note: Classical standardization conventionally dated to c. 500–400 BCE with grammarians such as Panini; the political and literary Sanskrit cosmopolis flourished across South and Southeast Asia from c. 300 to 1300 CE.

as_recorded.value: early centuries of the Common Era

where.modern_name: Patna, Bihar, India (stand-in pin for the classical Sanskrit cosmopolis across South and Southeast Asia; ancient Pataliputra)
where.historical_name: Pāṭaliputra, Magadha (imperial capital of the Maurya and Gupta empires, major center of classical Sanskrit courtly patronage)

importance.justification: The prestige language of learning and courts across South and Southeast Asia for about a thousand years (R3 D2 T4 L3).
